cultivar: Fuding Dabai, Meitan Taicha (local landrace) and Longjing 43
processing: Pan-fired flat green: single buds or bud-and-one-leaf shoots are fired and pressed flat in heated pans in the Longjing manner, mostly by machine, then dried at low temperature.
harvest_season: Early spring, from early March to around Qingming; the Guizhou plateau gives an early start, and nearly all top lots are pre-Qingming.
appearance_dry: Flat, straight, even buds in bright jade green with a light sheen.
appearance_wet: Plump single buds and tiny leaves, bright green, standing in the glass.
taste_profile: Fresh chestnut and sweet bean with a light, clean body and a soft savoury note; a tidy, bright green.

brewing.notes: Tall glass at 80 °C. Treat it like a Longjing with smaller leaf: light dose, water off the boil.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's early spring harvest, mostly pre-Qingming, in bud-only and bud-and-leaf grades; Guizhou's huge plantings keep prices moderate. The Meitan origin is protected, and the same style from elsewhere in the province is sold as Guizhou Cui Ya or by the shape name Que She. Drink within the year, kept cold and sealed.
description:
Meitan Cui Ya, 'jade bud', is the flagship green of Meitan county near Zunyi in northern Guizhou, which has quietly become one of China's biggest tea counties over the last two decades. It is a flat, Longjing-style bud tea, and it is the tea most likely to be in your cup when a cheap 'Dragon Well' turns out to be surprisingly good.

The style is honest about its inspiration: single buds or a bud with one small leaf, fired and pressed flat in heated pans, mostly by machine, and dried at low heat for a bright jade colour. The Guizhou plateau, high and cool with early springs and clean air, grows a tender, sweet bud that suits the format.

It drinks fresh and clean: chestnut and sweet bean, a light body, a soft savoury note and a quick sweetness. It is less deep than West Lake Longjing and less toasty, but at a fraction of the price it is a pleasure rather than a compromise. Brew it in a tall glass at 80 °C with a light dose; three steeps.

It is sold as the early spring harvest of the current year, almost all of it pre-Qingming because Guizhou picks from early March, in bud-only and bud-and-leaf grades. The Meitan origin is protected, and the same style from the rest of the province is sold as Guizhou Cui Ya or by the shape name Que She, 'sparrow tongue'. The main thing to watch is the label at the other end: this tea is often resold as Longjing, so if a 'Longjing' is very early, very cheap and very bright, it may well be this, and you can buy it honestly for less.

Guizhou's other styles, Duyun Mao Jian and the curly 'green gem' teas, make a good contrast to this one.
